citation.title: Nonparametric identification is not enough, but randomized controlled trials are

standing_assumptions:
Superpopulation setting: an i.i.d. sample with a binary outcome, a binary treatment and one continuous covariate; all probabilities and expectations are over repeated i.i.d. samples. Transcribed from the page images. Printed page = PDF page + 1 (Observational Studies 11.1 (2025): 3-16; PDF p. 1 is a cover sheet).

(S1) Sampling model, Section 2, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'We assume that we have an i.i.d. sample $(W_i, Y_i, X_i)$ from some large population, where $Y_i$ and $X_i$ are binary, and $W_i$ is drawn from a continuous distribution (either known or unknown). As above, $Y_i$ is the outcome, $X_i$ is the treatment, and $W_i$ is the covariate. We restrict our attention to simple treatment assignment mechanisms that assign treatments independently between units with unequal treatment probabilities that depend only on the unit’s own observed covariate $W_i$. We formalize this restriction as an unconfoundedness assumption, as stated below. The fact that the support of $W_i$ is large (here uncountable) is central to our discussion, because it ensures that all units will have unique covariate values.'

(S2) Consistency, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'For our discussion, we invoke the consistency assumption (c.f., the stable unit treatment value assumption), $Y_i = (1 - X_i)Y_i(0) + X_iY_i(1)$,'

(S3) Unconfoundedness, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'and unconfoundedness, $Y_i(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X_i \mid W_i, \quad \forall x \in \{0, 1\}$.'

(S4) Propensity score and positivity, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'We define the propensity score function as $\pi(w) = \Pr(X_i = 1|W_i = w)$, and assume that positivity holds, meaning that $\delta < \pi(W_i) < 1 - \delta$ with probability one for some positive $\delta$.'

(S5) Estimand, p. 5 (PDF p. 4): 'Without loss of generality, the parameter of interest is the average potential outcome under treatment: $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$.'

(S6) Known propensity score, p. 6 (PDF p. 5): 'In an RCT, all determinants of treatment are known because the experimenter decides how treatment is assigned. We assume full compliance with the treatment assignment and complete ascertainment of the outcome $Y_i$. This means that unconfoundedness holds by design, because the treatment assigned to unit $i$ only depends on its covariate $W_i$. Similarly, positivity can also be guaranteed to hold by design. [...] in an RCT, the propensity score function, $\pi(w)$, is known to the researcher, since it is specified by the experimental design.' Footnote 2, p. 6: 'We continue to maintain the assumption that the sample is i.i.d. to ensure comparability with the observational setting.' Propositions 2, 3 and 4 each open with 'Suppose the propensity scores are known.' Proposition 1 concerns the case in which $\pi$ is not known.

(S7) Estimators. Horvitz-Thompson, Proposition 2, p. 6 (PDF p. 5): $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$. Cross-fitted regression estimator, p. 7 (PDF p. 6): 'Let $s : [n] \to \{0, 1\}$ be a deterministic function that partitions the sample into two groups of roughly equal size, such as $s(i) = \lfloor (2i + n)/2n \rfloor$. Let $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ be two estimators of the regression function $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|W_i = w]$, where $\hat g_0$ is estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 1\}$ and $\hat g_1$ is estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 0\}$. The regression-based estimator of $\mu$ is then $\hat\mu_R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{X_i[Y_i - \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]}{\pi(W_i)} + \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)\right\}$.'

(S8) Notation that is not printed in the paper and is used in the targets below (the validators' notation; definitions, not extra assumptions): $m(w) = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i = w]$ (the paper writes this regression function out, p. 7); $F_W$, the distribution of $W_i$; $\mathbf{W} = (W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_n)$ (printed, p. 16); $\mu_{\mathbf{W}} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} m(W_i)$; $q(w) = (1 - \pi(w))/\pi(w)$. The validators take the vectors $(W_i, Y_i(0), Y_i(1), X_i)$ to be i.i.d. across $i$ and the potential outcomes to be binary; the paper says only that $Y_i$ and $X_i$ are binary, and with consistency, unconfoundedness and positivity this gives $Y_i(1) \in \{0, 1\}$ almost surely, so $0 \le m(w) \le 1$. $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 6); restated in Appendix A, p. 15 (PDF p. 14)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement: p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] Proposition 3 Suppose the propensity scores are known. Then a finite-sample-valid $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is $\hat\mu \pm \sqrt{\xi \log(2/\alpha)/2n}$, where $\xi = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}$ is the mean of the square inverse of the propensity scores. [Appendix A, p. 15 (PDF p. 14)] 'The proposition states $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}\right) \le \alpha$.' [Counterexample from the validators (v1 derivation.md sections 2 and 4-6; v2 derivation.md section 4); not in the paper.] Let $n = 100$ and $\alpha = 1/10^7$. For each unit independently let $W_i \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$; let $\pi(w) = 13/20$ for $w \le 3/5$ and $\pi(w) = 99/100$ for $w > 3/5$; let $X_i \mid W_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi(W_i))$; let $Y_i(1) = \mathbf{1}\{W_i \le 3/5\}$ and $Y_i(0) = 0$; and let $Y_i = (1 - X_i)Y_i(0) + X_iY_i(1) = X_i\mathbf{1}\{W_i \le 3/5\}$. Every standing assumption holds: the sample is i.i.d.; $Y_i$ and $X_i$ are binary; $W_i$ has a continuous distribution; consistency holds by construction; unconfoundedness holds because both potential outcomes are functions of $W_i$; positivity holds with $\delta = 1/200$, since $1/200 < 13/20 < 199/200$ and $1/200 < 99/100 < 199/200$; and the propensity score function is known. The estimand is $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)] = 3/5$. Let $K = \sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{W_i \le 3/5\}$ and $S = \sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{W_i \le 3/5\}X_i$. Then $\hat\mu = S/65$, $\hat\mu - \mu = (S - 39)/65$, and $\xi = \xi_K$ with $\xi_k = \frac{1}{100}\left(\frac{400k}{169} + \frac{10000(100 - k)}{9801}\right)$. Each unit falls in one of three categories, $\{W_i \le 3/5, X_i = 1\}$, $\{W_i \le 3/5, X_i = 0\}$, $\{W_i > 3/5\}$, with probabilities $39/100$, $21/100$, $40/100$, so for $0 \le s \le k \le 100$, $\Pr(K = k, S = s) = \binom{100}{k}\binom{k}{s}\frac{39^{s}\,21^{k-s}\,40^{100-k}}{100^{100}}$. In state $(k, s)$ the closed printed interval excludes $\mu$ exactly when $\frac{(s - 39)^2}{65^2} > \frac{\xi_k\log(2 \cdot 10^7)}{200}$, that is, when $T_{k,s} := \frac{200(s - 39)^2}{4225\,\xi_k} > \log(20{,}000{,}000)$. Of the $5151$ states, exactly $1946$ satisfy this strict inequality, and $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| > \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}\right) = \sum_{(k,s):\,T_{k,s} > \log(2\cdot 10^7)}\Pr(K = k, S = s) = 1.19792910697956254725767226256\ldots \times 10^{-7} > \frac{119}{10^9} > \frac{1}{10^7} = \alpha$. Hence the printed interval covers $\mu$ with probability strictly less than $1 - \alpha$, and a fortiori $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}\right) > \alpha$, contradicting the display that Appendix A gives as the content of the proposition.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Estimator: Proposition 2, p. 6 (PDF p. 5)] $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$. [$\xi$: Proposition 3, p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] $\xi = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}$, a random variable (a function of the sampled covariates). [Estimand: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$, the population mean. [Finite-sample valid: p. 7 (PDF p. 6), the sentence before the proposition] 'This confidence interval is finite-sample valid, meaning that its coverage is guaranteed to be greater or equal to its nominal level even in small samples.' Coverage is over repeated i.i.d. samples (S1); Appendix A (p. 15, PDF p. 14) restates the claim as $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}\right) \le \alpha$. [Radius] The root covers the whole expression $\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n$, in which $/2n$ is division by $2n$ (the last display of the proof rewrites $-2\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n$ as $-\{n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}\}\log(2/\alpha)$) and $\log$ is the natural logarithm (the proof uses $2\exp(-\log(2/\alpha)) = \alpha$). [Level] The paper states no restriction on $\alpha$; the validators read the claim for every $0 < \alpha < 1$ and every $n \ge 1$. [Propensity score, positivity, consistency, unconfoundedness: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] as in the standing assumptions (S2)-(S4).
canonical_claim.note: P046-E001 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json), so this target, P046-T2 and P046-T3 have priority 2. Both validators give this design and the same exact probability (v1 derivation.md sections 2, 4-6; v2 derivation.md section 4; both re-runs upheld). The exact noncoverage probability is the integer 11979291069795625472576722625601454579193931030581441019247695948117336197717708252113744670235734049700195915329948439938976976688794607547282140972800735873954434550061258658968400997158933003 divided by $100^{100}$ (runs/P046/validate/P046-E001/v1/artifact/certificate.json, key failure_mass_numerator_over_100_pow_n; also v1/artifact/output.txt). The failing states are listed in runs/P046/validate/P046-E001/v1/artifact/failure_ranges.csv (for each $k$, a lower and an upper range of $s$) and in runs/P046/validate/P046-E001/v2/artifact/cells.csv. Every $T_{k,s}$ is rational; the validators classify the states with the certified enclosure $16.811242831518265097543172304248 < \log(2\cdot 10^7) < 16.811242831518265097543172304249$, obtained from $\log(2\cdot 10^7) = 24\log 2 + \log(156250/131072)$ and the series $\log x = 2\sum_{j \ge 0} z^{2j+1}/(2j+1)$, $z = (x-1)/(x+1)$ (v1 section 5); no $T_{k,s}$ lies within $0.0087$ of the enclosure, so the strict and the weak inequality give the same set. A lower bound on the noncoverage probability needs only the 1946 failing states and an upper bound on the logarithm. The same design also gives a positive-probability covariate event on which the conditional display of the proof fails (v1 section 3): on $\{W_i > 3/5 \text{ for every } i\}$, of probability $(2/5)^{100}$, $\hat\mu = 0$ and the printed event occurs with conditional probability one whenever $\log(2/\alpha) < 2n(3/5)^2(99/100)^2 = 88209/1250$, which holds at $\alpha = 10^{-7}$ and at $\alpha = 0.05$; the simpler instance of that step is P046-T2. Not established and not part of the target: undercoverage at a conventional level. In this same design the exact noncoverage is $0.01380528935979$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ and $0.003614098219106$ at $\alpha = 0.01$, both below $\alpha$ (v2 section 7). In writing this target the failing-state count, the exact numerator and both comparisons were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic from the formulas in the statement; they agree with the certificate.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 3, the conditional Hoeffding display, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed step: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 3, p. 16 (PDF p. 15)] 'The Horvitz–Thompson estimator can be written $\hat\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i$, where $A_i = [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$. Because the outcome is binary, the bound $0 \le A_i \le [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}$ holds with probability one. Recall that $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mu$, so by Hoeffding’s inequality, $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge \sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n} \,\middle|\, \mathbf{W}\right) \le 2\exp\left(\frac{-2\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}[n\pi(W_i)]^{-2}}\right)$.' The proof then writes the right-hand side as $2\exp\left(\frac{-\left\{n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}\right\}\log(2/\alpha)}{n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}}\right) = 2\exp\Big(-\log(2/\alpha)\Big) = \alpha$. [Counterexample from the second validator (v2 derivation.md section 3); not in the paper.] Let $n = 100$ and $\alpha = 1/20$. For each unit independently let $W_i \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$, $\pi(w) = 9/10$ for every $w$, $X_i \mid W_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(9/10)$, $Y_i(1) = \mathbf{1}\{W_i \ge 1/2\}$, $Y_i(0) = 0$ and $Y_i = (1 - X_i)Y_i(0) + X_iY_i(1)$. Every standing assumption holds (positivity with $\delta = 1/20$; unconfoundedness because the potential outcomes are functions of $W_i$; the propensity score is known). Then $\mu = 1/2$ and $\xi = 100/81$ for every sample. The event $E = \{W_i < 1/2 \text{ for all } i\}$ has probability $2^{-100} > 0$. For every covariate vector in $E$ and every treatment vector, $Y_i = 0$ for all $i$, so $\hat\mu = 0$ and $|\hat\mu - \mu| = 1/2$, while the squared printed radius is $\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n = \frac{\log 40}{162} < \frac{1}{4}$. Hence on $E$ the left-hand side of the printed conditional display equals $1$, while its right-hand side equals $2\exp(-\log 40) = 1/20 = \alpha$: the displayed inequality fails on a set of covariate vectors of positive probability. The reason is the centring: on $E$, $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu \mid \mathbf{W}] = \mu_{\mathbf{W}} = n^{-1}\sum_{i} m(W_i) = 0 \ne 1/2 = \mu$, with $m(w) = \mathbf{1}\{w \ge 1/2\}$.

[Radius] The root covers the whole expression $\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n$, in which $/2n$ is division by $2n$ (the last display of the proof rewrites $-2\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n$ as $-\{n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}\}\log(2/\alpha)$) and $\log$ is the natural logarithm (the proof uses $2\exp(-\log(2/\alpha)) = \alpha$). [Propensity score, positivity, consistency, unconfoundedness: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] as in the standing assumptions (S2)-(S4). [Summands and covariate vector: Appendix A, p. 16 (PDF p. 15)] $A_i = [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$, $\hat\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i$, $\mathbf{W} = (W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_n)$. canonical_claim.note: Counterexample to a step of the printed proof (the conditional Hoeffding inequality centred at $\mu$), not by itself to Proposition 3: the event has probability $2^{-100}$ and the propensity score here is constant, a case in which the printed interval is valid unconditionally (v2 section 7: with $\pi(W_i) = p$, $\xi = p^{-2}$ is deterministic and unconditional Hoeffding for $X_iY_i/p \in [0, p^{-1}]$ gives exactly the printed radius). The counterexample to the proposition itself is P046-T1. The step fails at a conventional level ($\alpha = 0.05$). The validator certifies $\log 40/162 < 1/4$ with a rational bound on the logarithm (v2 section 5; it suffices that $\log 40 < 40.5$). The first validator gives the same failure in the design of P046-T1 (v1 section 3). The step that is true, and that the corrected proof uses, is in P046-T3 (i)-(ii): conditional on $\mathbf{W}$ the estimator has mean $\mu_{\mathbf{W}}$, and $\Pr(|\hat\mu - \mu_{\mathbf{W}}| \ge t \mid \mathbf{W}) \le 2\exp(-2nt^2/\xi)$.

canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 6); proof in Appendix A, pp. 15-16 (PDF pp. 14-15)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected Proposition 3; the printed statement is on p. 7 (PDF p. 6). The correction replaces the radius $\sqrt{\xi\log(2/\alpha)/2n}$ by $(\sqrt{\xi} + 1)\sqrt{\log(4/\alpha)/(2n)}$ and the conditional-only proof by a two-error argument; estimand, estimator and assumptions are unchanged. From Sol's smallest repair and the validators' derivations (v1 section 7, v2 section 6).] Under the standing assumptions (S1)-(S5), suppose the propensity scores are known. Then for every $n \ge 1$ and every $0 < \alpha < 1$, a finite-sample-valid $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$ is $\hat\mu \pm (\sqrt{\xi} + 1)\sqrt{\log(4/\alpha)/(2n)}$, where $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$ and $\xi = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}$; that is, $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge (\sqrt{\xi} + 1)\sqrt{\frac{\log(4/\alpha)}{2n}}\right) \le \alpha$. [Corrected proof, each step part of the target.] Write $c = \sqrt{\log(4/\alpha)/(2n)}$, $A_i = [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$, $m(w) = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i = w]$ and $\mu_{\mathbf{W}} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} m(W_i)$. (i) Conditional centre: $\mathrm{E}[A_i \mid \mathbf{W}] = \frac{\mathrm{E}[X_iY_i(1) \mid W_i]}{n\pi(W_i)} = \frac{\mathrm{E}[X_i \mid W_i]\,\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i]}{n\pi(W_i)} = \frac{m(W_i)}{n}$, so $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu \mid \mathbf{W}] = \mu_{\mathbf{W}}$ and $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mathrm{E}[\mu_{\mathbf{W}}] = \mathrm{E}[m(W_i)] = \mu$. (ii) Conditional Hoeffding, correctly centred: conditional on $\mathbf{W}$ the $A_i$ are independent with $0 \le A_i \le [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}$, so for every $t \ge 0$, almost surely, $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu_{\mathbf{W}}| \ge t \mid \mathbf{W}\right) \le 2\exp\left(\frac{-2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}[n\pi(W_i)]^{-2}}\right) = 2\exp(-2nt^2/\xi)$; with $t = \sqrt{\xi}\,c$ the bound is $2\exp(-2nc^2) = 2\exp(-\log(4/\alpha)) = \alpha/2$, and since $\xi$ is a function of $\mathbf{W}$, taking expectations gives $\Pr(|\hat\mu - \mu_{\mathbf{W}}| \ge \sqrt{\xi}\,c) \le \alpha/2$. (iii) Sampling of the covariates: the $m(W_i)$ are i.i.d., lie in $[0, 1]$ and have mean $\mu$, so by Hoeffding's inequality $\Pr(|\mu_{\mathbf{W}} - \mu| \ge c) \le 2\exp(-2nc^2) = \alpha/2$. (iv) Triangle inequality and union bound: off the two events, $|\hat\mu - \mu| \le |\hat\mu - \mu_{\mathbf{W}}| + |\mu_{\mathbf{W}} - \mu| < (\sqrt{\xi} + 1)c$, hence $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge (\sqrt{\xi} + 1)c\right) \le \Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu_{\mathbf{W}}| \ge \sqrt{\xi}\,c\right) + \Pr\left(|\mu_{\mathbf{W}} - \mu| \ge c\right) \le \alpha$; no independence between the two events is used. (v) Width: positivity gives $\sqrt{\xi} < \delta^{-1}$, so the radius is less than $(\delta^{-1} + 1)\sqrt{\log(4/\alpha)/(2n)}$ and, for fixed $\alpha$, the width of the interval is $O(n^{-1/2})$. [Alternative correction with a known bound.] If a fixed number $b > 0$ is known with $\pi(W_i) \ge b$ almost surely, then for every $n \ge 1$ and $0 < \alpha < 1$, $\hat\mu \pm b^{-1}\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)/(2n)}$ is a finite-sample-valid $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $\mu$: the variables $Z_i = X_iY_i/\pi(W_i)$ are i.i.d., lie in $[0, b^{-1}]$ and have mean $\mu$, so by Hoeffding's inequality $\Pr\left(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge b^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\alpha)}{2n}}\right) \le \alpha$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Estimator: Proposition 2, p. 6 (PDF p. 5)] $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$. [$\xi$: Proposition 3, p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] $\xi = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-2}$. [Estimand: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)]$. [Finite-sample valid: p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] 'its coverage is guaranteed to be greater or equal to its nominal level even in small samples'; $\Pr(|\hat\mu - \mu| \ge r) \le \alpha$ implies that the closed interval $\hat\mu \pm r$ covers $\mu$ with probability at least $1 - \alpha$. [Summands and covariate vector: Appendix A, p. 16 (PDF p. 15)] $A_i = [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$, $\hat\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i$, $0 \le A_i \le [n\pi(W_i)]^{-1}$ with probability one, $\mathbf{W} = (W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_n)$. [Not printed; validators' notation] $m(w) = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1) \mid W_i = w]$ and $\mu_{\mathbf{W}} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} m(W_i)$. [Hoeffding's inequality, in the form the validators use (v1 section 1); the paper invokes it by name on pp. 7 and 16] for independent $Z_i$ with $a_i \le Z_i \le b_i$: $\Pr\left(\left|\sum_i Z_i - \sum_i \mathrm{E}Z_i\right| \ge t\right) \le 2\exp\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_i(b_i - a_i)^2}\right)$; in step (ii) it is applied under the conditional law given $\mathbf{W}$, using independence across units, $X_iY_i = X_iY_i(1)$ (consistency), unconfoundedness and $\mathrm{E}[X_i \mid W_i] = \pi(W_i)$. [Standing assumptions: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] i.i.d. sample, binary $Y_i$ and $X_i$, consistency, unconfoundedness, positivity $\delta < \pi(W_i) < 1 - \delta$.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P046-E001): 'Preserve the population target and assumptions, replace the radius by $(\sqrt{\xi}+1)\sqrt{\log(4/\alpha)/(2n)}$, and replace the proof by correctly centered conditional Hoeffding at error level alpha/2 plus unconditional Hoeffding for $\mu_{\mathbf W}-\mu$ at error level alpha/2, followed by the triangle inequality and union bound. This is a local repair, not a claim of an optimal radius. A known fixed bound b>0 with pi(W)>=b also permits the alternative radius $b^{-1}\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)/(2n)}$.' Repair cost recorded by the validators: weaker conclusion (a wider interval); no new distributional assumption, the same estimand, computable from the known propensity scores of the sampled units, and the same root-n width rate. Both validators derive the corrected interval in full (v1 section 7; v2 section 6) and both re-runs upheld them. Merely replacing $\mu$ by $\mu_{\mathbf{W}}$ in the printed proposition would validate the printed radius but change the estimand; that is not the selected repair. The alternative needs a numerical lower bound $b$ that is known and valid; the first form uses only the observed known scores. Related printed text on p. 7 that the corrected interval restores: 'has the benefit of being finite-sample valid, therefore guaranteeing uniform validity. Note that the width of the interval decreases at the parametric rate $O(n^{-1/2})$.' Rated Moderate, hence priority 2.

canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement: p. 8 (PDF p. 7)] Proposition 4 Suppose the propensity scores are known. Then: [...] (c) If $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ are parameterized by a finite number of parameters and estimated by minimizing the empirical weighted mean square error of the outcome regression with weights $w_i = [\pi(W_i)]^{-2}[1 - \pi(W_i)]$, then $\hat\mu_R$ is at least as asymptotically efficient as the Horvitz–Thompson estimator $\hat\mu$. [Counterexample from the validator (derivation.md sections 2-5); not in the paper.] For each unit independently let $W \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)$, $L = \mathbf{1}\{W \le 1/2\}$ and $Z \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/10)$ with $Z$ independent of $W$. Conditional on $W$, let $X$ be independent of $Z$ with $\pi(W) = \Pr(X = 1 \mid W) = 1/4$ if $L = 1$ and $3/4$ if $L = 0$. Let $Y(0) = Y(1) = LZ$ and $Y = (1 - X)Y(0) + XY(1) = LZ$. Every standing assumption holds: outcome and treatment are binary, the covariate is continuous, consistency holds by definition, unconfoundedness holds because $X$ is independent of $Z$ given $W$, positivity holds with $\delta = 1/8$, and the propensity score function is known. The estimand is $\mu = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)] = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{10} = \frac{1}{20}$. Working family, with one unrestricted real parameter: $\mathcal{G} = \{g_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\}$, $g_\theta(w) = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}\{w \le 1/2\} + \theta\,\mathbf{1}\{w > 1/2\}$. (a) Empirical fit. The weight is $12$ where $L = 1$ and $4/9$ where $L = 0$, and $Y_i = 0$ where $L_i = 0$, so for every training set $T$, $Q_T(\theta) = \sum_{i \in T} X_i\frac{1 - \pi(W_i)}{\pi(W_i)^2}[Y_i - g_\theta(W_i)]^2 = 12\sum_{i \in T:\,L_i = 1} X_i(Z_i - 1/2)^2 + \frac{4}{9}\sum_{i \in T:\,L_i = 0} X_i\theta^2 = C_T + \frac{4}{9}N_T\theta^2$, where $C_T$ does not depend on $\theta$ and $N_T$ is the number of treated units of $T$ with $L_i = 0$. Hence $\hat\theta_T = 0$ minimizes $Q_T$ for every sample (uniquely when $N_T \ge 1$; when all parameters tie, the rule selects $\hat\theta_T = 0$, which is a minimizer), and both cross-fitted fits are exactly $\hat g_0 = \hat g_1 = g_*$ with $g_*(w) = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}\{w \le 1/2\}$. (b) Population criterion: $\mathrm{E}\left[X\frac{1 - \pi(W)}{\pi(W)^2}(Y - g_\theta(W))^2\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1 - \pi(W)}{\pi(W)}(Y(1) - g_\theta(W))^2\right] = \frac{3}{8} + \frac{1}{6}\theta^2$, uniquely minimized at $\theta = 0$; the empirical fits equal the population minimizer $g_*$ with zero error at every sample size. (c) Summands. Let $H = XY/\pi(W)$ and $A = X[Y - g_*(W)]/\pi(W) + g_*(W)$. Where $L = 0$, $H = A = 0$; where $L = 1$, $H = 4XZ$ and $A = 4XZ + \frac{1}{2}(1 - 4X)$, so $A = 1/2$ on $\{L = 1, X = 0\}$ (probability $3/8$), $A = -3/2$ on $\{L = 1, X = 1, Z = 0\}$ (probability $9/80$) and $A = 5/2$ on $\{L = 1, X = 1, Z = 1\}$ (probability $1/80$). Then $\mathrm{E}[H] = \mathrm{E}[A] = \frac{1}{20}$, $\mathrm{E}[H^2] = \frac{1}{5}$, $\mathrm{E}[A^2] = \frac{17}{40}$, $\mathrm{Var}(H) = \frac{79}{400}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(A) = \frac{169}{400}$. (d) Estimators. Because the fitted function is the same deterministic function for every training sample, $\hat\mu_R = n^{-1}\sum_{i} A_i$ exactly, and $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i} H_i$; both are means of i.i.d. bounded variables. For every $n$: $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu] = \mathrm{E}[\hat\mu_R] = \mu$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu) = \frac{79}{400n}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_R) = \frac{169}{400n}$; and $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu - \mu) \Rightarrow N(0, 79/400)$, $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu_R - \mu) \Rightarrow N(0, 169/400)$. The adjusted estimator is strictly less asymptotically efficient than the Horvitz–Thompson estimator: excess $n$-scaled variance $9/40$, variance ratio $169/79$. (e) What the family lacks: it does not contain the zero function, and zero is not in its weighted $L^2$ closure, since $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1 - \pi(W)}{\pi(W)}g_\theta(W)^2\right] = \frac{3}{8} + \frac{1}{6}\theta^2 \ge \frac{3}{8}$ for every $\theta$. In the notation of P046-T5, $\mathrm{Var}(Y(1)) = \frac{19}{400}$, $R(0) = \frac{3}{20}$ and $R(g_*) = \frac{3}{8}$, so $R(g_*) - R(0) = \frac{9}{40} > 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Estimators: p. 6 (PDF p. 5) and p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$; $s : [n] \to \{0, 1\}$ a deterministic function that partitions the sample into two groups of roughly equal size; $\hat g_0$ estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 1\}$ and $\hat g_1$ using $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 0\}$; $\hat\mu_R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{X_i[Y_i - \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]}{\pi(W_i)} + \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)\right\}$. [Weights: Proposition 4(c), p. 8 (PDF p. 7)] $w_i = [\pi(W_i)]^{-2}[1 - \pi(W_i)]$. [Empirical weighted mean square error of the outcome regression] Not written as a formula in the paper. The validator reads it, with the estimator definition and the citation the paper gives for part (c) (Section 3 of Cao et al. 2009: weighted least squares on the treated, i.e. complete, cases), as $Q_T(g) = \sum_{i \in T} X_i w_i [Y_i - g(W_i)]^2$ over the training fold $T$; dividing by a positive count or weight total does not change the minimizer. [Parameterized by a finite number of parameters] Not defined further; the paper's remark after the proposition (p. 8) says 'in (c), $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ need not converge to the true regression function', so misspecified families are allowed, and nothing restricts the family to a linear span or requires it to contain the zero function. [At least as asymptotically efficient] Not defined in the paper; read as: the variance of the limiting normal distribution of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu_R - \mu)$ is no larger than that of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu - \mu)$. In the counterexample $n\,\mathrm{Var}$ of each estimator is constant in $n$ and equals that limiting variance. [Standing assumptions: p. 5 (PDF p. 4)] (S1)-(S5).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for every $n \ge 1$ in the counterexample law: (i) the eight atoms of $(L, Z, X)$ have probabilities $\Pr(L = l, Z = z, X = x) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{z}\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^{1-z}\pi_l^{x}(1 - \pi_l)^{1-x}$ with $\pi_1 = 1/4$, $\pi_0 = 3/4$ (validator section 2); (ii) $Q_T(\theta) = C_T + \frac{4}{9}N_T\theta^2$ for every training set, so $\hat\theta_T = 0$ is a minimizer (section 3); (iii) the population criterion equals $\frac{3}{8} + \frac{1}{6}\theta^2$ (section 3); (iv) $\mathrm{E}[H] = \mathrm{E}[A] = 1/20$, $\mathrm{E}[H^2] = 1/5$, $\mathrm{E}[A^2] = 17/40$, $\mathrm{Var}(H) = 79/400$, $\mathrm{Var}(A) = 169/400$ (section 4); (v) $\hat\mu_R = n^{-1}\sum_i A_i$ and $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_i H_i$ with i.i.d. summands, so $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_R) = \frac{169}{400n} > \frac{79}{400n} = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu)$ and $n\,\mathrm{Var}$ is constant in $n$ (section 4). The only limit statement is the i.i.d. central limit theorem for bounded summands, which identifies $169/400$ and $79/400$ as the asymptotic variances.
canonical_claim.note: P046-E002 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json; validator verdict confirmed_in_part: Proposition 4(c) is false as printed, while the nearby sentence on p. 7 that adjustments 'can be constructed so that they cannot harm' asymptotic precision is an existence claim that remains true). Priority 3. The validator's check.py also enumerates all 64 samples at $n = 2$ and all 4096 samples at $n = 4$ with actual opposite-fold weighted fitting, empty treated folds included, and obtains $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu) = 79/800, 79/1600$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_R) = 169/800, 169/1600$ (artifact/check-output.txt). The counterexample also holds with the parameter restricted to $[0, 1]$. A repaired construction in the same law (validator section 6): the family $g_{a,\theta} = aL + \theta(1 - L)$ contains zero, has risk $R(g_{a,\theta}) = \frac{3}{2}a^2 - \frac{3}{10}a + \frac{3}{20} + \frac{1}{6}\theta^2$, unique minimizer $a = 1/10$, $\theta = 0$ and limiting variance $73/400 < 79/400$. The atom moments in (c) were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic in writing this target. The printed part (c) is not listed as a separate as-printed target because the finding is below Moderate; it is quoted here and in P046-T5.

canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected Proposition 4(c); the printed statement is on p. 8 (PDF p. 7). The correction adds two conditions on the working family and its fit, (i) and (ii) below; the estimand, the estimator, the weights and the conclusion are unchanged. From Sol's smallest repair and the validator's derivation (sections 5-6).] Under the standing assumptions (S1)-(S5), suppose the propensity scores are known. (c) Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a fixed working family of square-integrable functions of $w$ parameterized by a finite number of parameters, and let $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ be estimated by minimizing over $\mathcal{G}$ the empirical weighted mean square error of the outcome regression with weights $w_i = [\pi(W_i)]^{-2}[1 - \pi(W_i)]$, that is $Q_T(g) = \sum_{i \in T} X_i w_i [Y_i - g(W_i)]^2$, on the training sets $T = \{i \in [n] : s(i) = 1\}$ for $\hat g_0$ and $T = \{i \in [n] : s(i) = 0\}$ for $\hat g_1$. Write $q(w) = (1 - \pi(w))/\pi(w)$ and $R(g) = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1 - \pi(W)}{\pi(W)}(Y(1) - g(W))^2\right]$. Suppose that (i) $\mathcal{G}$ contains the zero function, or the zero function lies in the closure of $\mathcal{G}$ in the weighted norm $\|g\|_q = \mathrm{E}[q(W)g(W)^2]^{1/2}$; and (ii) as $n \to \infty$, $\|\hat g_j - g_*\|_{L^2(F_W)} \to 0$ in probability for $j = 0, 1$, where $g_* \in \mathcal{G}$ is a deterministic minimizer of $R$ over $\mathcal{G}$. Then $\hat\mu_R$ is at least as asymptotically efficient as the Horvitz–Thompson estimator $\hat\mu$: $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu_R - \mu) \Rightarrow N(0, V(g_*))$ and $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu - \mu) \Rightarrow N(0, V(0))$, where $V(g) = \mathrm{Var}(Y(1)) + R(g)$, and $V(g_*) \le V(0)$. [Weaker direct condition for a particular law, also from Sol's repair] the conclusion holds whenever (ii) holds for some deterministic limit $g_*$ with $R(g_*) \le R(0)$; condition (i) is used only to obtain this inequality.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Estimators: p. 6 (PDF p. 5) and p. 7 (PDF p. 6)] $\hat\mu = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\pi(W_i)]^{-1}X_iY_i$; $s : [n] \to \{0, 1\}$ a deterministic function that partitions the sample into two groups of roughly equal size, such as $s(i) = \lfloor (2i + n)/2n \rfloor$; $\hat g_0$ and $\hat g_1$ 'two estimators of the regression function $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|W_i = w]$, where $\hat g_0$ is estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 1\}$ and $\hat g_1$ is estimated using observations $\{i \in [n] : s(i) = 0\}$'; $\hat\mu_R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{X_i[Y_i - \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)]}{\pi(W_i)} + \hat g_{s(i)}(W_i)\right\}$. [Weights: Proposition 4(c), p. 8 (PDF p. 7)] $w_i = [\pi(W_i)]^{-2}[1 - \pi(W_i)]$; the paper adds (p. 8) 'the weights are known because they depend solely on the propensity scores'. [Empirical weighted mean square error] Not written as a formula in the paper; read as the weighted squared error over the treated units of the training fold, $Q_T(g) = \sum_{i \in T} X_i w_i [Y_i - g(W_i)]^2$ (validator section 3). [Not printed; validator's notation] $q(w) = (1 - \pi(w))/\pi(w)$; the population weighted risk $R(g) = \mathrm{E}[q(W)(Y(1) - g(W))^2]$; $V(g) = \mathrm{Var}(A_g)$ for the fixed-prediction summand $A_g = X[Y - g(W)]/\pi(W) + g(W)$; $F_W$ the distribution of $W_i$; folds $I_j = \{i : s(i) = j\}$. Under positivity $q$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, so convergence in $L^2(F_W)$ and in the weighted norm are equivalent. [At least as asymptotically efficient] Not defined in the paper; read as: the variance of the limiting normal distribution of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu_R - \mu)$ is no larger than that of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu - \mu)$. [Asymptotic sequence] Not specified in the paper; $n \to \infty$ under a fixed law satisfying (S1)-(S5), with the two folds of roughly equal size.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: All exact for a fixed law satisfying (S1)-(S5); derived in the validator artifact, sections 5-6; none is printed in the paper. Write $T = Y(1)$. (a) For a fixed square-integrable $g$: $A_g = X[Y - g(W)]/\pi(W) + g(W) = T + \left(\frac{X}{\pi(W)} - 1\right)(T - g(W))$ (using $XY = XT$), $\mathrm{E}[A_g \mid W, T] = T$ and $\mathrm{Var}(A_g \mid W, T) = q(W)(T - g(W))^2$, the latter from $\mathrm{Var}(X/\pi(W) \mid W, T) = (1 - \pi(W))/\pi(W)$; hence $\mathrm{E}[A_g] = \mu$ and $V(g) = \mathrm{Var}(A_g) = \mathrm{Var}(T) + R(g)$. (b) The Horvitz–Thompson summand is $A_0 = XY/\pi(W)$, so $\mathrm{Var}(XY/\pi(W)) = \mathrm{Var}(T) + R(0)$. (c) The population version of the weighted criterion is the risk: $\mathrm{E}\left[X\frac{1 - \pi(W)}{\pi(W)^2}(T - g(W))^2\right] = R(g)$. (d) Zero as benchmark: $R(g) - R(0) = -2\mathrm{E}[q(W)Tg(W)] + \mathrm{E}[q(W)g(W)^2]$ and $|\mathrm{E}[qTg]| \le \sqrt{\mathrm{E}[qT^2]\,\mathrm{E}[qg^2]}$; so if $g_k \in \mathcal{G}$ with $\mathrm{E}[q g_k^2] \to 0$ then $R(g_k) \to R(0)$, and a minimizer $g_*$ of $R$ over $\mathcal{G}$ has $R(g_*) \le R(g_k)$ for every $k$, hence $R(g_*) \le R(0)$ and $V(g_*) \le V(0)$. (e) Cross-fitting remainder: with $e_j = \hat g_j - g_*$ and $D_j = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I_j}\left(1 - \frac{X_i}{\pi(W_i)}\right)e_j(W_i)$, $\hat\mu_R = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_{g_*,i} + D_0 + D_1$ exactly; conditional on the training fold of $\hat g_j$ the summands of $D_j$ are independent with mean zero and second moment $\mathrm{E}[q e_j^2]$, so $\mathrm{Var}(\sqrt{n}D_j \mid \text{training}) = \frac{|I_j|}{n}\mathrm{E}[q(W)e_j(W)^2] \le \mathrm{E}[q(W)e_j(W)^2]$. The limit steps resting on these: conditional Chebyshev gives $\sqrt{n}D_j \to 0$ in probability under (ii), and the i.i.d. central limit theorem applies to the bounded-variance summands $A_{g_*,i}$ and $A_{0,i}$.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P046-E002): 'Add that the working family contains the zero predictor, or zero lies in its weighted L2 closure, and that both cross-fitted predictions converge in L2 to a deterministic population weighted-risk minimizer in that fixed family. For a particular law, the weaker direct condition is that the limiting prediction's weighted risk is at most the zero predictor's risk. The separate existence sentence needs no change.' Repair cost recorded by the validator: minor regularity condition; it adds no assumption that the working model is true and does not change the estimand. Freely parameterized linear spans already contain zero, and any family can be augmented with zero. The conditions are sufficient, not necessary: zero inclusion is not needed for improvement under every particular law. The validator's counterexample (P046-T4) shows the printed part (c) fails without (i) even when (ii) holds exactly. Rated Minor; the author's instruction is that the corrected statement of every mathematical error is a target, so it is listed at priority 3. The statement is asymptotic; (a)-(e) are its finite lemmas.
